q: What is RAG and why use it?
short: Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves relevant chunks from an external knowledge base at question time, adds them to the prompt and generates an answer grounded in them: current and private knowledge, citations, fewer hallucinations, no retraining.

q: Top-K vs thresholding?
short: Top-K keeps a fixed number of highest-scoring chunks regardless of quality; thresholding keeps all above a score bar, adapting to quality. Top-K can include weak chunks or miss needed ones; thresholds can return too many or none.

q: Compute available tokens and chunks for 8,192 context, 300 system, 220 query, 512-token chunks.
short: 8,192 − 520 = 7,672 available; ⌊7,672/512⌋ = 14 chunks (a 15th would overflow).
follow: Effect of 1,000 tokens of chat history?

q: How many chunks for 18,200 tokens, size 600, overlap 120?
short: Stride = 480; ⌈18,200/480⌉ = ⌈37.9⌉ = 38 chunks (the last is partial).

q: Define retrieval precision and recall.
short: Precision = relevant retrieved / all retrieved (noise control); recall = relevant retrieved / all relevant in the golden set (coverage).

q: Why chunk documents with overlap?
short: Whole documents exceed the context and dilute similarity; chunks allow targeted retrieval. Overlap keeps sentences and ideas that straddle boundaries intact in at least one chunk.

q: When does Graph RAG beat vector RAG?
short: When the answer is a relationship or requires multi-hop reasoning across entities (how are A and B related? what is affected downstream?); for single-entity facts or textual similarity, vectors suffice and graphs add needless hops.
mistakes: Building a KG for every use case.

q: What is agentic RAG?
short: An LLM agent decomposes a complex question into sub-goals and loops plan → retrieve → reason, re-querying when something is missing, until it can answer with citations.
mistakes: Assuming one retrieval is always enough.

q: Why does re-ranking matter?
short: First-stage retrievers (bi-encoders) are fast but approximate; near-tied scores (0.990 vs 0.991) make a hard cut arbitrary and can drop the answer chunk. A cross-encoder re-ranker scores query–chunk pairs jointly and reorders candidates before the final cut.
follow: Does it fit the latency budget?

q: Latency budget 2,500 ms; embedding 150, retrieval 420, generation 1,600. Can you add a 400 ms re-ranker?
short: Used 2,170, remaining 330 ms: a 300 ms re-ranker fits; 400 ms doesn't unless another stage is sped up (cache embeddings, smaller generator, fewer candidates).

q: Explain why long conversations degrade.
short: Each turn consumes the fixed context window; past ~80–90% usage systems compact older turns into summaries, which is lossy, so original constraints and details disappear and hallucination risk rises.

q: Interpret: retrieve 1,000 chunks of which 10 are relevant (all 10 relevant found).
short: Precision 0.01, recall 1.0: the answer is present but drowned in noise, and the context budget is wasted; tighten the threshold or re-rank.

q: Vector DB vs knowledge graph for retrieval?
short: Vector DB: unstructured chunks, dense similarity, mostly single-hop, low explainability, moderate effort, good for general document Q&A. KG: structured nodes/edges, traversal/Cypher, multi-hop, high explainability, high integration effort, good for connected domain logic.
follow: How to keep them in sync?

q: How can a text-only system do multimodal RAG?
short: Convert every modality to text first: describe images and charts, extract tables as text, transcribe audio/video; then embed and retrieve the narrations with ordinary text RAG. Cheaper, but loses fidelity (numbers in charts must be captured correctly).
detail: True multimodal embeddings avoid the loss.

q: Name three KG–LLM synergy patterns.
short: KG-enhanced LLMs (retrieve verified facts/paths for answers), LLM-augmented KGs (LLMs extract triples to build or complete graphs), and synergised systems where both continuously improve each other.
detail: Graph RAG is the first pattern.

q: Design a RAG assistant for a university's policy documents.
short: Chunk the documents by headings with overlap; embed with a good sentence encoder; hybrid BM25 + dense retrieval; threshold plus cap, then cross-encoder re-rank; prompt with 'answer only from context, cite sections, say if unknown'; golden-set evaluation of retrieval P/R and answer faithfulness; refresh the index when documents change; access controls per document.
mistakes: Dumping whole documents into the prompt.

q: How do you evaluate a RAG system end to end?
short: Retrieval: precision/recall (or recall@K, MRR) against golden chunks. Generation: faithfulness (claims supported by retrieved text), answer relevance, correctness vs reference answers; plus latency and cost. Frameworks for RAG metrics and human spot checks help.
detail: Evaluate components separately to localise failures.
follow: How to build a golden set cheaply?

q: What security risks does RAG introduce?
short: Prompt injection hidden in retrieved documents, leakage of documents users shouldn't see (missing access control in retrieval), poisoned knowledge bases, and over-trust in retrieved but outdated content. Treat retrieved text as data, enforce permissions at retrieval, and log sources.
example: 'Ignore previous instructions' hidden inside a document.
mistakes: Letting retrieved text override system instructions.

q: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context windows?
short: RAG: changing/private facts with citations, cheap updates. Fine-tuning: behaviour, style, format, domain language; poor for frequently changing facts. Long context: simple for moderate document sets but costly per query, slower, and models use mid-context information less reliably. Often combined.

q: What makes agentic RAG hard to operate?
short: Unbounded loops and costs, compounding errors across steps, agents agreeing with false corrections ('failing politely'), tool failures, and weak observability. Mitigate with step budgets, verification steps, per-agent metrics and traces, and human review for high-stakes outputs.
detail: Design the checks as carefully as the pipeline.
